y-m-11-01.title: What number comes after 2, 4, 8?
y-m-11-01.topic: Rules in number patterns: deciding whether the same beginning fixes the next number as just one
y-m-11-01.goal: Understand that the first few numbers of a pattern may not fix the rule as just one, make next numbers using different rules, and say what else you need to know.
y-m-11-01.material: Jihu laid out number cards in a row. The first three are 2, 4, 8. Jihu said, “The next card is definitely 16!” All the numbers on the cards are natural numbers, and there is a rule that decides the next number from the number before it.
y-m-11-01.thinking.0: Checking whether the claim is really 'definitely' true
y-m-11-01.thinking.1: Making your own different rule that explains the same data
y-m-11-01.thinking.2: Judging whether the information is enough and saying what more information is needed
y-m-11-01.prereq.0: Looking at the difference and the multiple between neighboring numbers in a number pattern (3rd–4th grade level)
y-m-11-01.prereq.1: Basics of calculating with natural numbers
y-m-11-01.s.s1.prompt: What do you think about Jihu's words “The next card is definitely 16”?
y-m-11-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write side by side what changes and how when going from 2 to 4 and from 4 to 8.
y-m-11-01.s.s1.hint.1: Besides looking at 'how many times', also write the way of looking at 'how much was added', and compare the two ways.
y-m-11-01.s.s1.o.a: 16 is right. Because 2, 4, 8 grow by doubling the number before
y-m-11-01.s.s1.r.a: It is true that 2, 4, 8 fit the doubling rule. But you have not yet tested whether there is another rule that makes the same three numbers.
y-m-11-01.s.s1.o.b: You can know whether it is 16 only after checking whether there is another rule that makes 2, 4, 8
y-m-11-01.s.s1.r.b: This is the idea of not stopping after finding one rule, but testing whether another rule makes the same number pattern.
y-m-11-01.s.s1.o.c: The numbers keep getting bigger, so the next card can be anything bigger than 8
y-m-11-01.s.s1.r.c: You only used the fact that it gets bigger and did not look at how much bigger it gets each time. How about looking at the relationship between neighboring numbers?
y-m-11-01.s.s1.o.d: There are only three cards, so we cannot say there is a rule and we cannot know the next number
y-m-11-01.s.s1.r.d: You did not use the condition 'there is a rule'. If there is a rule, you can look for the possible rules from the three cards.
y-m-11-01.s.s1.explain: 2, 4, 8 can be made by the rule 'double the number before', and also by the rule 'the number added to the number before grows by 2, as 2, 4'. The next number differs depending on the rule, so it is hard to say it is 16 from just three cards.
y-m-11-01.s.s2.prompt: Let's test Jihu's words. Make 2 different numbers that could come after 2, 4, 8. The next number must follow one of these rules: (가) a rule that multiplies the number before by some number of times each time, or (나) a rule where the number added to the number before increases by the same amount each time.
y-m-11-01.s.s2.hint.0: First find 'how many times' and 'how much was added' going from 2 to 4 and from 4 to 8.
y-m-11-01.s.s2.hint.1: Write what number you get when you apply each rule to 8 one more time.
y-m-11-01.s.s2.ok.c1: The next number is a natural number greater than 8.
y-m-11-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Make the next number a natural number greater than 8.
y-m-11-01.s.s2.ok.c2: It is a number that follows one of the two rules.
y-m-11-01.s.s2.fail.c2: This number does not come after 2, 4, 8 by either rule (가) or rule (나). Apply each of the two rules once to 8.
y-m-11-01.s.s2.explain: With rule (가), doubling, it is 16, which is 8 doubled. With rule (나), where the added number grows by 2 as 2, 4, 6, it is 8+6=14. From the same three numbers, the next number can be different.
y-m-11-01.s.s3.prompt: Jihu told the rule in words. “The number added to the number before grows by 2 each time.” By this rule, what is the number on the card right after 2, 4, 8?
y-m-11-01.s.s3.hint.0: Following the rule you were told, first write the numbers added in 2→4 and 4→8.
y-m-11-01.s.s3.hint.1: Next, write how the added number changes and add it to 8.
y-m-11-01.s.s3.r.a: You are still using the rule of continuing by doubling the number before. The rule you were just told is about the added number.
y-m-11-01.s.s3.r.b: You kept the added number at 4. In the rule you were told, the added number is different each time.
y-m-11-01.s.s3.r.c: This is the idea of continuing the added numbers as 2, 4, 6.
y-m-11-01.s.s3.r.d: You added 2 to 8. Continue the flow in which the added number grew from 2 to 4.
y-m-11-01.s.s3.explain: When the rule is given in words, the next number is fixed as just one. The added numbers are 2, 4, 6, so 8+6=14. When only a few numbers are given, the next number may not be fixed as just one, and it becomes fixed if you are told the rule or one more next number.

y-m-11-02.title: Looking at Minsu's equation in the apple box table
y-m-11-02.topic: Reading the correspondence of two quantities in a table and writing it as an equation (a relationship that grows by the same number)
y-m-11-02.goal: Test an equation that is right in only one cell of the table in all the cells and fix it, and write the same relationship as equations in two directions.
y-m-11-02.material:
A fruit shop sells apples in boxes. Each box holds the same number of apples. Minsu organized the number of boxes and the number of apples in a table.
When the number of boxes is 1, there are 5 apples; when the number of boxes is 2, there are 10 apples; when the number of boxes is 3, there are 15 apples.
Minsu said, “If you add 4 to the number of boxes, you get the number of apples.”
y-m-11-02.thinking.0: Finding the mistake in a generalization that is right in only one cell
y-m-11-02.thinking.1: Verifying an equation using several cells of the table
y-m-11-02.thinking.2: Writing the same relationship as a different equation
y-m-11-02.prereq.0: Reading a table of two quantities that change together (3rd–4th grade level)
y-m-11-02.prereq.1: Basics of calculating with natural numbers (3rd-grade level)
y-m-11-02.s.s1.prompt: Follow Minsu's thinking. Which line is hard to believe? Choose one line.
y-m-11-02.s.s1.hint.0: In each line, separate the lines that copy the numbers from the table as they are and the lines that draw a new conclusion.
y-m-11-02.s.s1.hint.1: Put the equation from the line that draws a new conclusion into the other cells of the table, and compare with the values in the table.
y-m-11-02.s.s1.line.0: If there is 1 box, there are 5 apples, and 1 plus 4 is 5.
y-m-11-02.s.s1.line.1: If there are 2 boxes, there are 10 apples.
y-m-11-02.s.s1.line.2: So I think adding 4 to the number of boxes always gives the number of apples.
y-m-11-02.s.s1.line.3: Using this equation for 3 boxes, 3 plus 4 gives 7 apples.
y-m-11-02.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is the problem. It was checked only in the first cell of the table (1 box) and then said 'always'. As a result, line 4 gave 7, but the table says 15 when there are 3 boxes. Lines 1 and 2 copy the table, so they are fine. Being right in one cell does not mean being right in every cell.
y-m-11-02.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the relationships that are right in all three cells of the table.
y-m-11-02.s.s2.hint.0: Put the numbers of the first, second, and third cells of the table into each equation in turn.
y-m-11-02.s.s2.hint.1: First cross out the equations that are not right in even one of the three cells.
y-m-11-02.s.s2.o.a: Number of boxes + 5 = number of apples
y-m-11-02.s.s2.r.a: 1+5=6, which is different from the 5 apples even in the first cell.
y-m-11-02.s.s2.o.b: Number of boxes × 5 = number of apples
y-m-11-02.s.s2.r.b: This is a choice that checked the three cells of the table with the relationship of multiplying the number of boxes by 5.
y-m-11-02.s.s2.o.c: Number of boxes × 2 + 3 = number of apples
y-m-11-02.s.s2.r.c: It is right in the first cell, but check it in the second cell (2 boxes).
y-m-11-02.s.s2.o.d: Number of apples ÷ 5 = number of boxes
y-m-11-02.s.s2.r.d: You read the same relationship in the backward direction too, finding the number of boxes from the number of apples.
y-m-11-02.s.s2.o.e: Number of apples − number of boxes = 4
y-m-11-02.s.s2.r.e: It is 4 only in the first cell. Find the difference in the second cell.
y-m-11-02.s.s2.explain: If you multiply the number of boxes by 5, you get the number of apples (1×5=5, 2×5=10, 3×5=15), and if you divide the number of apples by 5, you get the number of boxes. The two equations state the same relationship forward and backward. The other equations are right in only one or two cells.
y-m-11-02.s.s3.prompt: Minsu wants to fix his first equation. Write how it would be good to fix it and how you would check that the equation is right.
y-m-11-02.s.s3.hint.0: Put the number from the second cell of the table into the equation you made now.
y-m-11-02.s.s3.hint.1: First write the equation in words. 'When there is one more box, how many more apples are there?'
y-m-11-02.s.s3.placeholder: Example: To the number of boxes, ...
y-m-11-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you put the numbers in yourself to check that the fixed equation is right in other cells of the table, not only the first cell?
y-m-11-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain the relationship between the number of boxes and the number of apples using the words 'so many each'?
y-m-11-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you realize that it can also be said with a different equation?
y-m-11-02.s.s3.model.0: Fix it to the equation that multiplies the number of boxes by 5 (number of boxes × 5 = number of apples). I checked that all three cells of the table are right: 1×5=5, 2×5=10, 3×5=15.
y-m-11-02.s.s3.model.1: There are 5 in each box, so the number of apples grows by 5, as 5, 10, 15. So I write number of apples ÷ 5 = number of boxes, and I can check that 15÷5=3 gives 3 boxes correctly.
y-m-11-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that is written as a division equation and checked in at least one cell

y-m-11-03.title: Finding and fixing a rule from a bike rental price table
y-m-11-03.topic: Testing the rule each time information increases, and fixing the range when a new condition (maximum price) appears
y-m-11-03.goal: Test a rule made from a few cells of the table with a new cell, and when a new condition appears on the sign, fix the range in which the rule is right and make several cases.
y-m-11-03.material: You want to find out the prices at the park's bike rental shop. The price is decided by the time rented, and you can rent only in 1-hour units, exactly 1 hour, 2 hours, 3 hours, and so on. I will give you the information one piece at a time.
y-m-11-03.thinking.0: Making a guess from little data and adjusting how sure you are
y-m-11-03.thinking.1: Changing or keeping your judgment according to new information
y-m-11-03.thinking.2: Making several answers under a condition
y-m-11-03.prereq.0: Reading a table of two quantities that change together (3rd–4th grade level)
y-m-11-03.prereq.1: Calculating money in units of one thousand 원
y-m-11-03.s.s1.prompt: Each time the information increases by one piece, choose the suitable answer.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write the numbers of the cells you were told about in each step side by side in a table.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.hint.1: Tell apart whether the newly given information 'confirms the rule' or 'changes the range of the rule'.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.0.info: If you rent for 1 hour, it is 3000원, and if you rent for 2 hours, it is 4000원.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: How much will the price be if you rent for 3 hours?
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.0.after: The price went up by 1000원 between the two cells, so you can guess 3 hours will be 5000원. But there are only two cells of data, so it is not certain.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: 9000원. It is 3000원 for 1 hour, so 3 hours is 3 times that
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You calculated 3 times the price for 1 hour. But 2 hours is 4000원, not 6000원. Check whether it fits the two cells of the table.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: 5000원. It went up by 1000원 for each additional hour, so it will go up by 1000원 again
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is the idea of finding the amount of increase between the two cells and continuing it.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: 7000원. It is the 1-hour price plus the 2-hour price
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You added 3000원 and 4000원. Check whether this method gives the same value for the 1-hour and 2-hour prices too.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It seems like it will be 5000원, but there are only two cells, so I can't know until I see the 3-hour price
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You made a guess but also thought about the fact that the data is small.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.1.info: You confirmed that renting for 3 hours is 5000원 and renting for 4 hours is 6000원.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: Then how much will the price be if you rent for 10 hours?
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.1.after: All four cells fit 'number of hours + 2' (thousand 원). If you continue this rule, you can guess 10 hours is 12000원. It is also suitable to leave open that there may be conditions you do not know yet.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You only added the 1-hour price ten times. Check whether 4 hours is 12000원 in the table.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 14000원. It goes up by 8000원 from 6000원 for 4 hours
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Check how much it goes up while 6 more hours are added up to 10 hours.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: 12000원. It is the number of hours plus 2, with thousand 원 attached
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is the idea of finding a rule that fits all four cells and putting 10 hours into it.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.1.o.d: For hours not in the table the rule might change, so I can't decide now
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You left open the possibility that the rule changes even as data increases. First check whether the data so far lets you continue the calculation.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.2.info: The rental shop sign says, “Maximum price per day (within 24 hours): 10000원.” No matter how long you rent, the daily price does not go over 10000원.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: How much will the price be if you rent for 10 hours?
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.2.after: The 10-hour price found by the rule, 12000원, is bigger than the maximum price 10000원. So in reality you pay only 10000원. The rule 'number of hours + 2' (thousand 원) is right up to 8 hours (10000원), and after that the maximum price applies.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: There is a new condition, so I need to compare whether the value from the rule goes over 10000원
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This is the idea of comparing the new condition with the rule already found.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 12000원. The rule I found was right in four cells, so it stays as it is
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Think, together with the condition on the sign, about how far the range is in which the rule was right.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: 30000원. The 1-hour price keeps adding up over the day
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The sign tells a value that the daily price cannot go over.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.2.o.d: 10000원. The value from the rule is bigger than the maximum price, so you pay only the maximum price
y-m-11-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This is the idea of comparing the value from the rule with the maximum price and using the smaller one.
y-m-11-03.s.s1.reflect: How did your prediction change each time you learned the first two cells, the four cells, and the sign? Up to what range was the rule right? Tell apart whether the change was because of the data or because of the new condition.
y-m-11-03.s.s2.prompt: Make cases in which you end up paying exactly 10000원 within a day (within 24 hours). Write 3 different rental times t (in 1-hour units, 1 hour or more and 24 hours or less).
y-m-11-03.s.s2.hint.0: Change the hours to 1, 2, 3, … and write the prices in a table.
y-m-11-03.s.s2.hint.1: Separate what the actual price is when the value from the rule is 10000원 or less and when it goes over.
y-m-11-03.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a time within a day, in 1-hour units.
y-m-11-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Make the time a natural number from 1 to 24.
y-m-11-03.s.s2.ok.c2: With this time, the price is 10000원.
y-m-11-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The price for this time is not 10000원. Compare the value from the rule with the maximum price.
y-m-11-03.s.s2.explain: For 8 hours, the value from the rule is 10000원, and from 9 hours on, the value from the rule is bigger than 10000원, so you pay the maximum price 10000원. So any time from 8 hours to 24 hours is 10000원.

y-m-11-04.title: Cutting out a 3×3 block from a calendar
y-m-11-04.topic: Discovering the relationship between numbers that are neighbors across and down in the number pattern of a calendar
y-m-11-04.goal: Make your own examples to check that the sum of a 3×3 block in the calendar looks like a multiple of the middle number, and explain with pairing why it holds even when the number of cells in a row changes.
y-m-11-04.material:
This is the calendar of a month with 31 days. The 1st is a Sunday, and there are 7 cells in a row (Sun, Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat). The first row is 1~7, the second row is 8~14, the third row is 15~21, the fourth row is 22~28, and the fifth row is 29, 30, 31. Going one cell to the right makes the number 1 bigger, and going one cell down makes the number 7 bigger.
Harin cut out a square shape (9 cells) that is 3 cells across and 3 cells down from the calendar, added all 9 numbers, and said, “It seems to be a multiple of the middle cell's number!”
y-m-11-04.thinking.0: Checking an observation by making your own examples
y-m-11-04.thinking.1: Looking at the condition under which the relationship holds (the cells fit inside the calendar)
y-m-11-04.thinking.2: Explaining why it is so (the reason for the rule)
y-m-11-04.prereq.0: Looking at how the numbers change one cell to the right and one cell down in a number pattern (3rd–4th grade level)
y-m-11-04.s.s1.prompt: Make examples that check Harin's observation. Choose the middle cell's number m so that all 9 cells fit in the calendar as a square of connected cells, and write the sum s of all 9 numbers. Make 3 examples with different middle numbers.
y-m-11-04.s.s1.hint.0: Choose one middle cell in the calendar, and first write the three cells each in the upper row, middle row, and lower row.
y-m-11-04.s.s1.hint.1: Write the sum you found next to the middle number and compare the relationship between the two.
y-m-11-04.s.s1.ok.c1: The 9 cells fit inside the 1st to the 31st of the calendar.
y-m-11-04.s.s1.fail.c1: The rows above and below the middle cell must both be in the calendar. Choose the middle number again.
y-m-11-04.s.s1.ok.c2: The 9 cells connect as cells in the same rows.
y-m-11-04.s.s1.fail.c2: If the middle cell is a Saturday or Sunday, the cell to the right (or left) goes over to the next (or previous) row. Change the day of the week of the middle cell.
y-m-11-04.s.s1.ok.c3: The sum of the 9 cells is right.
y-m-11-04.s.s1.fail.c3: The sum of the 9 cells is different from the numbers in the calendar. Check again the 8 cells around the middle cell.
y-m-11-04.s.s1.explain: For example, if the middle is 10, the sum of the 9 cells is 90, for 13 it is 117, and for 18 it is 162. In the three examples, the sum is 9 times the middle number. If the middle cell is a Saturday or Sunday, the 9 cells do not connect as a square.
y-m-11-04.s.s2.prompt: If Harin's observation is right, what would the sum be in a calendar with 5 cells in a row instead of 7 (first row 1~5, second row 6~10, …) when 9 cells fit as a square?
y-m-11-04.s.s2.hint.0: In the 5-cell calendar, choose one middle cell and write the numbers of the cells above, below, left, and right.
y-m-11-04.s.s2.hint.1: Pair up the two cells on opposite sides of the middle cell and find their sum.
y-m-11-04.s.s2.o.a: It seems to be a multiple of the middle number only when the number of cells in a row is 7
y-m-11-04.s.s2.r.a: You think the rule exists because of the number 7. In the 5-cell calendar, write yourself how much bigger or smaller the cells above and below are than the middle.
y-m-11-04.s.s2.o.b: You need to know the number of cells in a row to decide how many times the middle number the sum is
y-m-11-04.s.s2.r.b: You thought it depends on the number of cells. Set the number of cells to 5 and write the cells above and below to check what happens.
y-m-11-04.s.s2.o.c: Even if a row has 5 cells, the sum is 9 times the middle number
y-m-11-04.s.s2.r.c: This is a judgment from thinking that the relationship between the cells above and below might be similar even when the number of cells changes.
y-m-11-04.s.s2.o.d: If a row has 5 cells, it becomes 5 times the middle number
y-m-11-04.s.s2.r.d: You thought the number of cells in a row is directly multiplied into the sum. Add the 9 numbers yourself in the 5-cell calendar to check.
y-m-11-04.s.s2.explain: No matter how many cells are in a row, with the middle cell as the reference, the cells above and below form a pair that are smaller and bigger by the same amount, and the left and right cells also form a pair. The sum of a pair is 2 times the middle number, so 4 pairs plus the middle is 9 times the middle number.
y-m-11-04.s.s3.prompt: Harin wonders why. When the middle number is m, pair up the cells two at a time or group them one row at a time, and explain why the sum of the 9 cells is a multiple of the middle number.
y-m-11-04.s.s3.hint.0: Compare the sum of the two cells on opposite sides of the middle cell with the middle number.
y-m-11-04.s.s3.hint.1: Group one row (three cells across) at a time and compare its sum with the number in the middle cell.
y-m-11-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: With middle number m, the cell above and the cell below are ...
y-m-11-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write clearly which cells pair up with each other, based on the middle number?
y-m-11-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write 'why it is so' in words that work for any cell, not just one example?
y-m-11-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you realize there is another way of explaining (grouping rows)?
y-m-11-04.s.s3.model.0: With middle number m, the cell above, m-7, plus the cell below, m+7, is 2m. The left m-1 and the right m+1 are also 2m, and the pairs on the two diagonals are also 2m. There are 4 pairs, so 8m, and adding the middle m gives 9m, that is, 9 times the middle number.
y-m-11-04.s.s3.model.1: If you add three cells across, the two sides are 1 less and 1 more, so it is 3 times the middle cell. The middle cells of the three rows are m-7, m, m+7, and their sum is 3m. So the whole is 3 times 3m, which is 9m, that is, 9 times the middle number.
y-m-11-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that explained by grouping rows

y-m-11-05.title: If one side doubles, does the other side double too?
y-m-11-05.topic: Comparing how the other quantity changes when one of two quantities that change together doubles
y-m-11-05.goal: Among four tables, pick out the cases where the other side exactly doubles when one side doubles, and explain with a counterexample that being right in two cases does not mean being right in all cases.
y-m-11-05.material:
Mina said, “When two things change together, if one side doubles, the other side definitely doubles too!” You want to check by looking at the tables of four situations. (All values follow a fixed rule.)
- Pencils: 1 pencil 500원, 2 pencils 1000원, 4 pencils 2000원
- Delivery: 1kg 3000원, 2kg 4000원, 4kg 6000원
- Area of a square: when a side is 1cm, 1cm²; when 2cm, 4cm²; when 4cm, 16cm² (read as square centimeters)
- Perimeter of a square: when a side is 1cm, 4cm; when 2cm, 8cm; when 4cm, 16cm
y-m-11-05.thinking.1: Finding the gap in an argument that generalizes from two cases
y-m-11-05.prereq.0: Reading how two quantities change together in a table (3rd–4th grade level)
y-m-11-05.prereq.1: Perimeter and area of a square
y-m-11-05.s.s1.prompt: In each table, the first number doubled from 1 to 2 and from 2 to 4. Choose all the situations in which the second number also becomes exactly 2 times both times.
y-m-11-05.s.s1.hint.0: For each table, write how many times the second number becomes when going from the first cell to the second cell.
y-m-11-05.s.s1.hint.1: Check the second cell to the third cell the same way, and keep only the tables that are 2 times both times.
y-m-11-05.s.s1.r.a: This is a choice that checked cell by cell whether the perimeter also becomes 2 times both times when a side doubles.
y-m-11-05.s.s1.r.b: Check how many times 3000원 becomes when going from the first cell to the second cell.
y-m-11-05.s.s1.r.c: There is a cell where the area becomes 4 times as big. Write how many times it becomes in each cell.
y-m-11-05.s.s1.r.d: This is a choice that checked that, since each pencil costs the same, when the number doubles, the price also doubles.
y-m-11-05.s.s1.explain: Pencils are 500원, 1000원, 2000원, which is 2 times both times, and the perimeter is 4, 8, 16, also 2 times both times. Delivery goes from 3000 to 4000, which is not 2 times, and the area goes from 1 to 4, which is 4 times.
y-m-11-05.s.s2.prompt: Read Mina's story and choose the line that is hard to believe.
y-m-11-05.s.s2.hint.0: Point out which table each line was said from.
y-m-11-05.s.s2.line.0: A pencil is 500원 for 1 and 1000원 for 2, so it doubles.
y-m-11-05.s.s2.line.1: The perimeter of a square also doubles when a side doubles.
y-m-11-05.s.s2.line.2: In both situations, when one side doubled, the other side doubled too.
y-m-11-05.s.s2.line.3: Therefore, however two things change together, when one side doubles, the other side definitely doubles too.
y-m-11-05.s.s2.explain: Line 4 is the problem. Lines 1~3 are really right in the two cases of the pencils and the perimeter. But being right in two cases does not mean it is definitely so 'however two things change together'. Looking at just one table, delivery or area, shows it does not double.
y-m-11-05.s.s3.prompt: How would you tell Mina? Using the numbers from the delivery or area table, explain that Mina's words are not always right, and guess and write what is the same about the pencils and the perimeter, where 'doubling gives doubling'.
y-m-11-05.s.s3.hint.0: In the delivery table, write the prices for 1kg and 2kg side by side and find how many times.
y-m-11-05.s.s3.hint.1: In the pencil and perimeter tables, look at the second number when the first number is 1 and compare with the other two tables.
y-m-11-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In the counterexample I gave, is it clear from the numbers that the first number doubles but the second number does not double?
y-m-11-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write knowing that being right in two cases does not guarantee 'definitely'?
y-m-11-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you test your guess about what is the same in the pencils and the perimeter with other numbers?
y-m-11-05.s.s3.model.0: For delivery, 1kg is 3000원, but 2kg is 4000원, not 6000원. So even if one side doubles, the other side does not always double. Pencils and perimeter seem to double because they are multiplication relationships with the same value for each one.
y-m-11-05.s.s3.model.1: For the area of a square, when a side goes from 1cm to 2cm, the area goes from 1cm² to 4cm², so it is 4 times, not 2 times. So Mina's words are wrong. It seems right only in cases like the perimeter, where it grows by exactly the same amount as the side grows.
y-m-11-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: What is the same is just a guess, so it does not have to be perfect

y-m-11-06.title: Ways to divide 24 candies into bags
y-m-11-06.topic: The correspondence between the number of bags and the number in one bag (when the total is fixed)
y-m-11-06.goal: Find the relationship in the table of how the number in one bag changes as the number of bags increases, make several ways that fit the conditions, and judge that in some cases it is impossible.
y-m-11-06.material:
You want to divide 24 candies into bags with the same number in each. You put in all the candies, with none left. Look at the table.
When the number of bags is 2, there are 12 in one bag; when the number of bags is 3, there are 8 in one bag; when the number of bags is 4, there are 6 in one bag.
y-m-11-06.thinking.0: Picking out the relationship that is right in the table (filtering out relationships that are right in only some cells)
y-m-11-06.thinking.1: Making several ways under a condition
y-m-11-06.prereq.0: Knowing the numbers in the multiplication table (2nd–3rd grade level)
y-m-11-06.prereq.1: Reading how two quantities change in a table
y-m-11-06.s.s1.prompt: Look at the table and choose the most suitable statement of the relationship between the number of bags and the number of candies in one bag.
y-m-11-06.s.s1.hint.0: For each of the three cells, write the sum, the difference, and the multiple of the two numbers.
y-m-11-06.s.s1.hint.1: Find the one that gives the same value in all three cells.
y-m-11-06.s.s1.o.a: Each time the number of bags goes up by 1, the candies in one bag go down by 4
y-m-11-06.s.s1.r.a: You only looked at the first two cells (12→8). Check whether it also went down by 4 in the third cell (8→6).
y-m-11-06.s.s1.o.b: If you add the number of bags and the number of candies in one bag, you always get the same number
y-m-11-06.s.s1.r.b: If you add the two numbers in each cell, you get 14, 11, 10. Check cell by cell whether the sums are the same.
y-m-11-06.s.s1.o.c: If you multiply the number of bags and the number of candies in one bag, you always get 24
y-m-11-06.s.s1.r.c: This is a choice that checked whether the value made from the two numbers is the same in the three cells.
y-m-11-06.s.s1.o.d: The number of candies in one bag is 6 times the number of bags
y-m-11-06.s.s1.r.d: It is 6 times only in the first cell (2→12). In the second cell, check whether 6 times the number of bags, 3, is 8.
y-m-11-06.s.s1.explain: In all three cells the product is 24: 2×12=24, 3×8=24, 4×6=24. This is because there are 24 candies in all. The sums and the numbers that went down are different in each cell.
y-m-11-06.s.s2.prompt: Find cases that are not in the table. Make 2 different ways to put all 24 candies in with none left over. The number of bags a is 5 or more, and each bag must hold b candies, which is 2 or more.
y-m-11-06.s.s2.hint.0: Like the three cells of the table, choose the number of bags one at a time and find how many must be in one bag to make 24.
y-m-11-06.s.s2.hint.1: Keep only the cells where the number of bags is 5 or more and one bag has 2 or more.
y-m-11-06.s.s2.var.b: Number of candies in one bag
y-m-11-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The number of bags is a natural number that is 5 or more, and the number of candies in one bag is a natural number that is 2 or more.
y-m-11-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Make the number of bags 5 or more, and the number of candies in one bag a natural number that is 2 or more.
y-m-11-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The total made from the number of bags and the number of candies in one bag is not 24. Check the relationship you found in the table.
y-m-11-06.s.s2.explain: The ways that fit the conditions are 6 bags with 4 each, 8 bags with 3 each, and 12 bags with 2 each. 4 bags with 6 each has a number of bags less than 5, and 24 bags with 1 each does not fit the condition that one bag must have 2 or more. (Ones with the numbers switched, like 6 bags with 4 each and 4 bags with 6 each, are different ways.)
y-m-11-06.s.s3.prompt: When there are 5 bags, can you put all 24 candies in with the same number in each and none left over?
y-m-11-06.s.s3.hint.0: Change the number in one bag to 1, 2, 3, … and write the total for 5 bags.
y-m-11-06.s.s3.hint.1: Look at whether there is a total that matches 24, or whether it skips past 24.
y-m-11-06.s.s3.o.a: You cannot put them in with the same number in each and none left over
y-m-11-06.s.s3.r.a: This is a judgment from checking the cases where both the number of bags and the number in one bag are natural numbers.
y-m-11-06.s.s3.r.b: 5 bags with 4 each is 20. Check whether all 24 candies were put in.
y-m-11-06.s.s3.r.c: 5 bags with 5 each is 25. Check whether there are 24 candies.
y-m-11-06.s.s3.o.d: It depends on how many go in each bag, so I can't tell
y-m-11-06.s.s3.r.d: You did not try the possible numbers one by one. Change the number to 1, 2, 3, … and write the total.
y-m-11-06.s.s3.explain: If you put 4 in each of 5 bags, it is 20, and if you put 5, it is 25, so neither matches 24 exactly. If you divide 24 equally into 5 bags, it does not divide evenly into a natural number, so it is impossible.

y-m-11-07.title: Minseo's and her older sister's ages, explaining to a younger cousin
y-m-11-07.topic: Explaining a relationship that adds a constant amount, like an age gap, with words and examples
y-m-11-07.goal: Find in a table a relationship in which a constant difference stays the same, like ages, find values, and rewrite the same relationship with words and examples that a 2nd-grade younger cousin can understand.
y-m-11-07.material: Minseo and her older sister count their ages from the day they were born in the same year (each year both of them get one year older). When Minseo is 4 years old, her sister is 7, when Minseo is 5, her sister is 8, and when Minseo is 6, her sister is 9. Minseo wants to tell her cousin, who is in 2nd grade of elementary school, how her sister's age is decided.
y-m-11-07.thinking.0: Finding the relationship (the difference is constant) in a table and predicting a new value
y-m-11-07.thinking.1: Changing an explanation to suit the listener
y-m-11-07.thinking.2: Checking with an example whether the explanation is right
y-m-11-07.prereq.0: Reading how two quantities change together in a table (3rd–4th grade level)
y-m-11-07.prereq.1: Basics of calculating with natural numbers
y-m-11-07.s.s1.prompt: When Minseo turns 10, how old will her sister be?
y-m-11-07.s.s1.hint.0: For each of the three cells of the table, find the difference between the sister's age and Minseo's age.
y-m-11-07.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the difference is the same or different in each cell, and compare how many years each of the two people gets older every year.
y-m-11-07.s.s1.r.a: You added the sister's first age 7 to Minseo's age 10. Check whether this method is right by applying it to the table where she is 7 when Minseo is 4.
y-m-11-07.s.s1.r.b: You saw it as 2 times Minseo's age. Check whether 2 times is right in the cells for 5 and 6 years old in the table.
y-m-11-07.s.s1.r.c: You took the age difference between Minseo and her sister to be 4. Find the difference between the two ages in one cell of the table.
y-m-11-07.s.s1.r.d: This is the idea of using the fact that both ages grow by the same amount each year.
y-m-11-07.s.s1.explain: In all three cells of the table, the sister is 3 years older than Minseo (7-4=3, 8-5=3, 9-6=3). Each year both get one year older, so the difference does not change. So when Minseo is 10, her sister is 13.
y-m-11-07.s.s2.prompt: Choose the most suitable explanation for Minseo to send to her cousin (2nd grade).
y-m-11-07.s.s2.hint.0: First check whether each explanation fits all three cells of the table.
y-m-11-07.s.s2.hint.1: Among the explanations whose relationship is right, choose the one that a 2nd-grade cousin can follow.
y-m-11-07.s.s2.o.a: My sister's age is “Minseo's age + 3”. You find it by adding 3 to my age, got it?
y-m-11-07.s.s2.r.a: The equation is right, but a cousin who is not used to symbols or equations may need words and an example first.
y-m-11-07.s.s2.o.b: My sister is about 2 times my age. When I'm 4, my sister is 7.
y-m-11-07.s.s2.r.b: You described the relationship from values that look similar in one cell. Check in the table how old my sister is when I'm 6.
y-m-11-07.s.s2.o.c: My sister is always 3 years older than me. When I'm 8, my sister is 11.
y-m-11-07.s.s2.r.c: You explained the relationship with words and an example that are easy for the listener to follow.
y-m-11-07.s.s2.o.d: My sister's age is always 7, even when my age changes.
y-m-11-07.s.s2.r.d: You said it does not change from looking only at the value in the first cell. Check in the table the sister's age when Minseo is 5.
y-m-11-07.s.s2.explain: c tells the right relationship in short words (always 3 years older) and an example, so even a 2nd-grade cousin can follow it. a is also a right relationship, but it may be hard to understand from the start for a cousin who is not used to equations. b and d are not right relationships.
y-m-11-07.s.s2.acc.0: The relationship is right. For a 2nd-grade cousin, it is even better to add words and an example.
y-m-11-07.s.s3.prompt: Now become Minseo and write the explanation to send to your cousin. Say how the sister's age is decided, and also tell how old the sister is when Minseo is 20.
y-m-11-07.s.s3.hint.0: Using one cell of the table as an example, first write in one sentence 'how many years older the sister is'.
y-m-11-07.s.s3.hint.1: Write the process of finding the value for age 20 one step at a time so your cousin can follow it.
y-m-11-07.s.s3.placeholder: Example: My sister is ... than me
y-m-11-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write the relationship in easy words that your cousin can understand?
y-m-11-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you give an example that your cousin could try following by themselves?
y-m-11-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you put your explanation into other cells of the table to check that it is right?
y-m-11-07.s.s3.model.0: My sister is always 3 years older than me. When I'm 5, my sister is 8. So when I turn 20, my sister is 20 plus 3, which is 23 years old.
y-m-11-07.s.s3.model.1: The age gap between us is always 3 years. When I was 4, my sister was 7, and when I turn 20, it's 20+3=23, so my sister will be 23.
y-m-11-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: An explanation that wrote the equation only once

y-m-11-08.title: Will 100 appear in the pattern 3, 7, 11, 15…?
y-m-11-08.topic: Judging which numbers appear in a number pattern that grows by a constant amount
y-m-11-08.goal: In a number pattern with a fixed rule, judge which numbers appear without writing out the numbers, understand that the single clue 'odd' is not enough, and make a number that fits the conditions.
y-m-11-08.material: There is a number pattern. 3, 7, 11, 15, … This pattern continues by adding the same number to the number before. I will give you the information one piece at a time.
y-m-11-08.thinking.1: Telling apart a necessary condition and a sufficient condition (not every odd number appears)
y-m-11-08.thinking.2: Making a number that fits the conditions
y-m-11-08.prereq.0: Reading a rule that grows by 4 in a number pattern (3rd–4th grade level)
y-m-11-08.prereq.1: Telling apart even and odd numbers
y-m-11-08.s.s1.prompt: Each time the information increases by one piece, choose the suitable answer.
y-m-11-08.s.s1.hint.0: Write the numbers you were told in each step side by side, and mark whether each is odd or even and the difference from the number before.
y-m-11-08.s.s1.hint.1: Tell apart whether your judgment is 'solid evidence' or 'a plausible clue'.
y-m-11-08.s.s1.st.0.ask: What will the next number be?
y-m-11-08.s.s1.st.0.after: 3, 7, 11, 15 grow by 4, so you can guess the next is 19. This pattern was said to add the same number to the number before, so this guess is more natural than other rules.
y-m-11-08.s.s1.st.0.o.a: 21. The differences from the number before are 4, 4, 4, so next the increase will be 6
y-m-11-08.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You cannot find in the first four numbers a reason to think the difference, which keeps being 4, changes to 6. Check the difference cell by cell.
y-m-11-08.s.s1.st.0.o.b: 19. Because we have been adding 4 to the number before
y-m-11-08.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is the idea of using the fact that the difference between neighboring numbers is the same.
y-m-11-08.s.s1.st.0.o.c: 17. Odd numbers that are 2 bigger than the number before continue
y-m-11-08.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You chose 17, the odd number after 15. Compare with how much it increased going from 3 to 7 and from 7 to 11.
y-m-11-08.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It seems like 19, but there may be another rule that makes these four numbers
y-m-11-08.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is the idea of making a guess but also leaving open the possibility of other rules.
y-m-11-08.s.s1.st.1.info: I checked further, and the next two numbers were 19 and 23. This pattern starts from 3 and keeps going, growing by 4 like this.
y-m-11-08.s.s1.st.1.after: Starting from 3 and adding 4 is adding an even number to an odd number, so it stays odd. So the even number 100 does not appear. Writing them out one by one to check whether it skips past 100 is also a right method.
y-m-11-08.s.s1.st.2.info: Minho said, “100 doesn't appear because it's even, right? Then 99 is odd, so it will appear!”
y-m-11-08.s.s1.st.2.after: 99 is 3+4×24, so it appears as the 25th number. Odd is only a necessary clue for appearing, and not every odd number appears (for example, 5 and 9 do not appear in this pattern). The judgment that it must be checked separately is also suitable.
y-m-11-08.s.s1.reflect: At each step, what was the evidence for your judgment 'appears / does not appear'? In your own words, write why the clue 'odd' tells you that 100 does not appear but does not tell you that 99 appears.
y-m-11-08.s.s2.prompt: Write 2 different numbers that appear in this pattern (starting from 3 and growing by 4) and are greater than 200 and less than 220.
y-m-11-08.s.s2.hint.0: Think about a way of writing the numbers that grow by 4 from 3, skipping ahead until close to 200.
y-m-11-08.s.s2.hint.1: When checking whether a number appears, look at how many times of 4 it takes to reach that number from 3.
y-m-11-08.s.s2.var.a: A number that appears in the pattern
y-m-11-08.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a natural number greater than 200 and less than 220.
y-m-11-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Make it a natural number greater than 200 and less than 220.
y-m-11-08.s.s2.ok.c2: It is a number that appears in this pattern.
y-m-11-08.s.s2.fail.c2: This number does not appear in the pattern. Check whether it is a number that starts from 3 and grows by 4. Some odd numbers do not appear.
y-m-11-08.s.s2.explain: The numbers in the pattern grow by 4 from 3, so 203, 207, 211, 215, 219 are in this range. 205 is odd, but it does not appear in the pattern.

y-m-11-09.title: What day of the week will it be in 50 days?
y-m-11-09.topic: Finding the day of the week some days later using a repeating rule (the cycle of the days of the week)
y-m-11-09.goal: Using the rule that the same day of the week comes back every 7 days, find the day of the week some days later, find and fix the mistake of treating 50 as the same day of the week as 49 because they are similar, and then make several numbers of days that fit the conditions.
y-m-11-09.material: Today is Thursday. The days of the week keep going around in the order Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Jiho wants to find out “What day of the week will it be in 50 days?” Read Jiho's solution.
y-m-11-09.thinking.0: Finding a wrong generalization in a repeating rule
y-m-11-09.thinking.1: Applying a rule to a new situation
y-m-11-09.thinking.2: Making several numbers of days that fit the conditions
y-m-11-09.prereq.0: The order of the days of the week and counting 'some days later', one week is 7 days (3rd–4th grade level)
y-m-11-09.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line in Jiho's solution that is hard to believe.
y-m-11-09.s.s1.hint.0: In each line, write how many days later the 'day when the same day of the week comes back' really is.
y-m-11-09.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the day of the week 49 days later and 50 days later are the same or different by counting on one day at a time.
y-m-11-09.s.s1.line.0: After 7 days, the same day of the week comes back. In 7 days it is Thursday.
y-m-11-09.s.s1.line.1: In 14 days, and in 21 days, it is Thursday too.
y-m-11-09.s.s1.line.2: In 49 days it is also Thursday. 50 is close to 49, so in 50 days it is also Thursday.
y-m-11-09.s.s1.line.3: Therefore in 50 days it is Thursday.
y-m-11-09.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is the problem. The statement that it is Thursday in 49 days is right. But 50 is not 49, so you cannot say it is the same day of the week. The numbers being close is not evidence for the same day of the week. Line 4 is a conclusion made by trusting line 3, so it is also wrong. We will find out what day of the week it is in 50 days in the next question.
y-m-11-09.s.s2.prompt: What day of the week will it be in 50 days?
y-m-11-09.s.s2.hint.0: Among the numbers of days when the same day of the week comes back, find the one closest to 50.
y-m-11-09.s.s2.hint.1: From the day of the week after that number of days, keep counting on for the remaining days.
y-m-11-09.s.s2.r.a: You treated 50 days as the same day of the week as 49 days later. Think about what happens when one more day passes after 49 days.
y-m-11-09.s.s2.r.b: This is the idea of adding the days left over after the number of days when the same day of the week comes back to the day of the week.
y-m-11-09.s.s2.r.c: This is the idea of taking the leftover days to be 2 days. Count how many days apart 49 days later and 50 days later are.
y-m-11-09.s.s2.r.d: This is the idea of counting one day backward from 49 days later. Think about whether 50 days later is earlier or later than 49 days later.
y-m-11-09.s.s2.explain: 49 days later is Thursday, and 50 days later is the next day, so it is Friday. You can read it as 7 days seven times making 49 days, with one day left over.
y-m-11-09.s.s3.prompt: When today is Thursday, make 3 different numbers of days after which it is Saturday. (The number of days d is a natural number from 1 to 60.)
y-m-11-09.s.s3.hint.0: When today is Thursday, write the days of the week 1 day later, 2 days later, 3 days later in order, and find the number of days at which it first becomes Saturday.
y-m-11-09.s.s3.hint.1: Also check the days of the week for the numbers of days you get by adding 7 days at a time to that number.
y-m-11-09.s.s3.ok.c1: It is a number of days from 1 to 60.
y-m-11-09.s.s3.fail.c1: Make the number of days a natural number from 1 to 60.
y-m-11-09.s.s3.ok.c2: After this number of days, it is Saturday.
y-m-11-09.s.s3.fail.c2: After this number of days, it is not Saturday. Think about how many days it takes to get from Thursday to Saturday, and what happens when a week passes.
y-m-11-09.s.s3.explain: 2 days after Thursday is Saturday. The same day of the week comes back every 7 days, so 9 days, 16 days, 23 days, … are also Saturday. Within 60 days, 2, 9, 16, 23, 30, 37, 44, 51, 58 days later are Saturday.
